text: Raúl Alfonsín served as president of Argentina from 1983 to 1989. He inherited an economic crisis rooted in the 1981–82 financial collapse, which left Argentina with a US$43 billion foreign debt and interest payments that consumed its entire US$3 billion trade surplus. Although the economy showed modest recovery in 1983 due to the lifting of wage freezes and the Central Bank's "Circular 1050," inflation soared to 400%, GDP per capita remained at its lowest level since 1968, and fixed investment was 40% below 1980 levels. Alfonsín appointed a center-left cabinet led by Foreign Minister Dante Caputo and Economy Minister Bernardo Grinspun, fulfilling campaign promises such as a nutritional assistance program for the 27% of Argentines living in poverty and reversing Bignone's blanket amnesty for human rights abuses and warrantless wiretapping. Defense Minister Raúl Borrás advised removing Fabricaciones Militares from military control, resulting in the retirement of 70 generals and admirals opposed to the transfer. He appointed playwright Carlos Gorostiza as Secretary of Culture and exiled scientist Dr. Manuel Sadosky as Secretary of Science and Technology, leading to hundreds of artists and scientists returning in 1984. Gorostiza abolished the National Film Rating Entity, contributing to a doubling of film and theatre production, and the film *La historia oficial* was released in April 1985 and won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Alfonsín established the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP), led by Ernesto Sábato, which documented 8,960 forced disappearances and presented its findings to the President on September 20; the report's victim count was lower than Amnesty International's estimate of 16,000 and the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo's estimate of 30,000. Alfonsín prosecuted members of leftist groups, including Mario Firmenich of the Montoneros, and pardoned former President Isabel Perón in May 1984 for her role in the Dirty War and alleged embezzlement, though his legislation for secret ballot labor union elections was rejected by the Senate by one vote. Relations with the United States deteriorated when Alfonsín ended support for the Contras, and two meetings with President Ronald Reagan failed to secure economic concessions. He initiated diplomatic contact with the United Kingdom, lifting British trade sanctions, and proposed a treaty with Chile to resolve the Beagle Channel border dispute, which was approved by voters with 82% support. Facing a foreign debt crisis worsened by high global interest rates, Alfonsín dealt with shattered business confidence and record budget deficits; GDP grew by 2% in 1984, but fixed investment declined and inflation rose to 700%. The federal budget had a US$10 billion shortfall in 1984 (13% of GDP), prompting the Central Bank to print money, which pushed inflation from 18% monthly to 30% in June 1985—the world's highest at the time. Economy Minister Juan Sourrouille introduced the Austral Plan, freezing prices and replacing the peso with the austral at 1,000 to one. Sharp budget cuts, especially in military spending, reduced it to about half of 1983 levels. A mechanism called desagio was introduced to compensate debtors affected by inflation drops, reducing inflation from 30% in June to 2% monthly by the end of 1985 and cutting the fiscal deficit by two-thirds. Military discontent grew, with bomb threats and sabotage blamed on hard-line officers, including former 1st Army Corps head Gen. Guillermo Suárez Mason, who fled to Miami after an October arrest order. Alfonsín sponsored the Trial of the Juntas, beginning on April 22, 1985, which prosecuted top military leaders for Dirty War crimes; in December, former President Jorge Videla and Navy Chief Emilio Massera received life sentences, and three others received 17-year sentences. Four defendants were acquitted, including former President Leopoldo Galtieri, who was later court-martialed in May 1986 for malfeasance during the Falklands War and sentenced to 12 years. For these actions, Alfonsín received the first Prize For Freedom of the Liberal International and the Human Rights Prize by the Council of Europe. In the November 1985 legislative elections, the UCR gained one seat in the Lower House and controlled 130 of 254 seats, while the Justicialists lost eight (leaving 103). In April 1986, Alfonsín announced a panel to plan the transfer of the capital to Viedma, 800 km south of Buenos Aires, proposing constitutional amendments for a parliamentary system with a prime minister, which was well received by the Lower House but opposed in the Senate. Economic concerns persisted, and a fall in global commodity prices in 1986 reduced the trade surplus from US$4.5 billion to half and inflation dropped to 50% by June 1986 (from 1,130% in June 1985), though it soon rose above 80%. GDP, which had declined 5% in 1985, grew 7% in 1986, driven by machinery purchases and consumer spending. Repeated wage freezes under Sourrouille caused real wages to fall by about 20%, triggering seven general strikes by the CGT. Alfonsín appointed conservative economist José Luis Machinea as Central Bank president, pleasing the financial sector but failing to stop capital flight, with affluent Argentines believed to hold over US$50 billion in overseas deposits. He made several state visits abroad to secure trade deals. His international reputation for human rights was damaged in December 1986 when Congress passed the Full Stop Law, limiting civil trials against roughly 600 officers to those indicted within 60 days of the law's passage. In 1987, during Easter weekend, a group known as the Carapintadas, loyal to Army Major Aldo Rico, staged a mutiny at Campo de Mayo and near Córdoba; Alfonsín negotiated their surrender and announced: "La casa está en orden y no hay sangre en Argentina. ¡Felices pascuas!" to signal the end of the crisis. His appointment of General Dante Caridi as Army Chief of Staff further strained military relations, and in June, Congress passed the Law of Due Obedience, granting immunity to officers implicated in crimes against humanity based on "due obedience," a law condemned by Amnesty International and effectively halting further prosecutions. Tensions were heightened by the suspicious death of Defense Minister Roque Carranza in 1986 and the September 1987 discovery of banker Osvaldo Sivak, kidnapped by police for a ransom of over one million US dollars. Despite this, Alfonsín passed the legalization of divorce, resolving the legal status of 3 million adults (1 in 6), and the Antidiscrimination Law of 1987, supported by Argentina's Jewish and Gypsy communities, earning him the Moisés Prize from the Argentine Jewish community. A severe drought in early 1987 reduced exports to their lowest level in a decade, canceling the trade surplus and creating a US$6 billion current account deficit. Alfonsín's debt negotiator, Daniel Marx, secured a record US$19 billion debt rescheduling (one-third of total debt), but speculators caused the austral to lose half its value between June and October, leading to higher inflation rising from 5% monthly to 20% in October. Unimpressed by the appointment of a Labor Minister from within the CGT, the union's leader Saúl Ubaldini called two more general strikes, and hundreds of sectoral strikes erupted. A positive relationship with Brazil's newly elected President José Sarney led to initial agreements for a common market with Uruguay in January 1988, including a special currency, the Gaucho, for subsidizing intra-regional exports. New Minister of Public Works Rodolfo Terragno advocated for privatizations to generate foreign exchange, resulting in the sale of Austral Airlines in September 1987. Subsequent instability and the Wall Street Crash of 1987 led to tax increases, and GDP rose 3% in 1987, driven by construction spending, though inflation reached 175% and real wages declined by about 10%, falling below 1983 levels. This economic downturn significantly weakened the UCR in local and legislative elections in September 1987, losing 13 seats in Congress (leaving 117) and losing its absolute majority in the Lower House and a majority in the Senate, suspending much of its legislative agenda, including the capital transfer plan. UCR governors fared poorly, with only two remaining, including Governor Armendáriz of Buenos Aires. Military discontent peaked when Major Aldo Rico escaped house arrest and organized a second mutiny in January 1988, which was quickly suppressed. The resulting tension and stagflation prompted Alfonsín to move the October 1989 elections five months earlier. During the May 1988 Justicialist Party convention, the CGT opposed frontrunner Buenos Aires Governor Antonio Cafiero, and Alfonsín supported pairing his struggling UCR (14 points behind in polls) against Cafiero's rival, Carlos Menem, a little-known governor from a small province. The primaries resulted in an upset, and Menem was nominated. The UCR selected Eduardo Angeloz, the centrist governor of Córdoba, as its candidate. The Austral Plan continued to fail, with inflation remaining at 15–20% monthly and reaching 27% in August. In April, foreign debt payments fell into arrears when Alfonsín ordered the Central Bank to halt payments. On August 3, Economy Minister Sourrouille announced the Plan Primavera, featuring a price truce with 53 wholesalers and a new wage freeze, triggering a violent September 9 general strike by the CGT at Plaza de Mayo. Despite the conviction of Banco Alas executives for fraud totaling US$110 million, their suspended sentences and the discovery of a "parallel customs" operation by National Customs Director Juan Carlos Delconte raised doubts about Alfonsín's anti-corruption efforts. Alfonsín obtained INTERPOL's cooperation to extradite fugitive Army Corps leader Gen. Guillermo Suárez Mason and Argentine Anticommunist Alliance mastermind José López Rega, who were returned to Argentina in 1987 to stand trial. The military relationship remained tense, with continued budget cuts and opposition to democracy leading to a third mutiny on December 1, supported by disaffected Coast Guard members; the leader, Col. Mohamed Alí Seineldín, was arrested after six days. In a compromise, Alfonsín announced a modest military budget increase and dismissed moderate General Dante Caridi as Army Chief of Staff. A January 23, 1989 attack on the Regiment of La Tablada by a leftist armed group killed 39 people, testing Alfonsín's improved military rapport, which allowed the military to prosecute the case, though allegations of torture emerged. Inflation fell from 27% in August to 5–10% monthly by the end of 1988, but GDP declined 2% and inflation rose to 380% while real wages continued to fall. Exports recovered, and the trade surplus rose to nearly US$4 billion. The Springtime Plan increasingly relied on reserves to stabilize the austral, which lost nearly all of its US$3 billion in reserves. On "Black Tuesday," February 7, 1989, the U.S. dollar gained 40% against the austral, triggering a sharp decline in the austral's value, which traded at 17 to the dollar in January and reached over 100 australes by May 14. Inflation, which had been below 10% monthly as late as February, surged to 78.5% in May, shattering records and leading to a landslide victory for Justicialist candidate Carlos Menem. Polling showed that economic anxieties were central to two-thirds of voters, and Menem won in 19 of 22 provinces.

Exports recovered, and the trade surplus increased to nearly US$4 billion. The Springtime Plan increasingly relied on its foreign reserves to support the austral, whose stability helped maintain lower inflation rates. In this process, the Central Bank depleted almost all of its US$3 billion in reserves. On "Black Tuesday," February 7, 1989, the Central Bank engaged in heavy trading, causing the U.S. dollar to rise by about 40% against the austral. The sharp depreciation of the austral undermined the country's fragile financial situation. Later that month, the World Bank recalled a major portion of a loan agreement from 1988, triggering a sharp decline in the austral's value: it traded at 17 to the dollar in January and reached over 100 australes per dollar by election day, May 14. Inflation, which had remained below 10% per month as late as February, surged to 78.5% in May, breaking records and contributing to a decisive victory for Justicialist candidate Carlos Menem. Polling showed that economic concerns were a top priority for two-thirds of voters, and Menem won in 19 of 22 provinces, while losing in the traditionally anti-Peronist Federal District (Buenos Aires). The nation's finances did not stabilize after the election as expected. The dollar doubled in value the following week, and on May 29, riots and looting erupted in the poorer areas of several cities, especially Rosario. Inflation continued to escalate: it reached 114% per month in June and 197% in July. Income poverty rose from about 30% to 47% during this period, and the economy contracted by 7% in 1989, bringing per capita GDP to its lowest level since 1964. Having committed to remain in office until December 10, Alfonsín transferred power to President-elect Menem on July 8 due to the ongoing financial crisis and escalating economic instability.
